claim: Information processing in cortical neuronal networks relies on properly balanced excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission.
source: Information processing in cortical neuronal networks relies on properly balanced excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a general statement about cortical network function that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: A ubiquitous motif for maintaining excitatory-inhibitory balance is the somatostatin interneuron (SOM-IN) feedback microcircuit.
source: A ubiquitous motif for maintaining this balance is the somatostatin interneuron (SOM-IN) feedback microcircuit.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about cortical circuit organization.

claim: Both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs to SOM-INs are strongly inhibited by GABABRs.
source: Whole-cell recordings from SOM-INs revealed that both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs are strongly inhibited by GABABRs
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SOM-INs shows that their inhibitory output is strongly suppressed by GABABRs.
source: while optogenetic activation of the interneurons shows that their inhibitory output is also strongly suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: GABABRs are highly expressed presynaptically at both input and output synapses of SOM-INs.
source: Electron microscopic analysis of immunogold-labelled freeze-fracture replicas confirms that GABABRs are highly expressed presynaptically at both input and output synapses of SOM-INs.
evidence: This is confirmed by electron microscopic immunogold labeling data.

claim: Activation of GABABRs selectively suppresses the recruitment of SOM-INs during gamma oscillations induced in vitro.
source: Activation of GABABRs selectively suppresses the recruitment of SOM-INs during gamma oscillations induced in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on network oscillations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Axonal GABABRs can functionally uncouple SOM-INs from the local network with implications for rhythmogenesis.
source: Thus, axonal GABABRs are positioned to efficiently control the input and output synapses of SOM-INs and can functionally uncouple them from local network with implications for rhythmogenesis and the balance of entorhinal versus intrahippocampal afferents.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings on GABABR function.

claim: Axonal GABABRs have implications for the balance of entorhinal versus intrahippocampal afferents.
source: Thus, axonal GABABRs are positioned to efficiently control the input and output synapses of SOM-INs and can functionally uncouple them from local network with implications for rhythmogenesis and the balance of entorhinal versus intrahippocampal afferents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of SOM-INs in gating inputs.

claim: SOM-INs innervate the distal apical dendritic tufts of PCs and INs.
source: A subpopulation of IN expresses the neuropeptide somatostatin (SOM) and innervates the distal apical dendritic tufts of PCs and INs (Katona et al., 1999; McBain et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SOM-INs act as a ubiquitous inhibitory feedback element in hippocampal and neocortical circuits.
source: SOM-INs act as a ubiquitous inhibitory feedback element in hippocampal and neocortical circuits, due to their preferential excitatory input from local PCs (Ali and Thomson, 1998; Blasco-Ibáñez and Freund, 1995; Lacaille et al., 1987; Müller and Remy, 2014; Shigemoto et al., 1996; Urban-Ciecko et al., 2018; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: SOM-INs receive preferential excitatory input from local PCs.
source: SOM-INs act as a ubiquitous inhibitory feedback element in hippocampal and neocortical circuits, due to their preferential excitatory input from local PCs (Ali and Thomson, 1998; Blasco-Ibáñez and Freund, 1995; Lacaille et al., 1987; Müller and Remy, 2014; Shigemoto et al., 1996; Urban-Ciecko et al., 2018; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Hippocampal SOM-INs contribute to the co-ordination of population activity in the theta frequency range (4–12 Hz).
source: Besides controlling dendritic excitability and synaptic plasticity at the single-cell level, hippocampal SOM-INs contribute to the co-ordination of population activity, particularly in the theta frequency range (4–12 Hz) (Gloveli et al., 2005b; Klausberger et al., 2003; Maccaferri and McBain, 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hippocampal SOM-INs contribute to population activity at higher frequencies in the beta and lower gamma band.
source: but also at higher frequencies in the beta and lower gamma band (Chen et al., 2017; Hakim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SOM-INs gate information flow between and within cortical areas.
source: They gate information flow between and within cortical areas (Leão et al., 2012; Naka et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SOM-INs support learning and memory processes.
source: and support learning and memory processes (Lovett-Barron et al., 2014; Abbas et al., 2018; Adler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cortical INs are strongly controlled by inhibitory mechanisms produced through both ionotropic GABAA receptors and metabotropic GABABRs.
source: Cortical INs are themselves strongly controlled by inhibitory mechanisms produced through both ionotropic GABAA receptors (GABAAR) and metabotropic GABABRs (Kulik et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: SOM-INs in CA1 of the hippocampus receive a strong GABAAR-mediated synaptic input from local INs, dominantly those expressing calretinin (CR) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
source: Indeed, SOM-INs in CA1 of the hippocampus have been shown to receive a strong GABAAR-mediated synaptic input from local INs, dominantly those expressing calretinin (CR) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) (Tyan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GABAAR-mediated inhibition onto INs has been linked to disinhibitory network mechanisms.
source: GABAAR-mediated inhibition onto INs more generally has been linked to disinhibitory network mechanisms (Acsády et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: GABAAR-mediated inhibition onto INs has been linked to the emergence of coherent oscillatory network activity.
source: and the emergence of coherent oscillatory network activity (Bartos et al., 2002; Bartos et al., 2007; Traub et al., 1999; White et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: GABABRs are ubiquitously expressed at both pre- and postsynaptic locations on PCs and INs.
source: despite the ubiquitous expression and abundant distribution of GABABRs at both pre- and postsynaptic locations on PCs and INs alike (Kulik et al., 2006; Kulik et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SOM-INs in CA1 express high levels of postsynaptic GABABRs.
source: We have recently shown that SOM-INs in CA1 express high levels of postsynaptic GABABRs and their activation does not activate Kir3 channels, but inhibit dendritic L-type (Cav1.2) calcium channels to suppress synaptic plasticity (Booker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Postsynaptic GABABR activation in SOM-INs does not activate Kir3 channels.
source: We have recently shown that SOM-INs in CA1 express high levels of postsynaptic GABABRs and their activation does not activate Kir3 channels, but inhibit dendritic L-type (Cav1.2) calcium channels to suppress synaptic plasticity (Booker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Postsynaptic GABABR activation in SOM-INs inhibits dendritic L-type (Cav1.2) calcium channels to suppress synaptic plasticity.
source: We have recently shown that SOM-INs in CA1 express high levels of postsynaptic GABABRs and their activation does not activate Kir3 channels, but inhibit dendritic L-type (Cav1.2) calcium channels to suppress synaptic plasticity (Booker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Presynaptic GABABR-mediated inhibition can efficiently control IN recruitment.
source: In fact, presynaptic GABABR-mediated inhibition would be able to efficiently control IN recruitment and to functionally uncouple them from the local network (Huh et al., 2016; Urban-Ciecko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Presynaptic GABABR-mediated inhibition can functionally uncouple INs from the local network.
source: In fact, presynaptic GABABR-mediated inhibition would be able to efficiently control IN recruitment and to functionally uncouple them from the local network (Huh et al., 2016; Urban-Ciecko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 63 visualized INs were confirmed to be immunoreactive for SOM.
source: After the recordings, immunoreactivity for SOM was confirmed in 63 visualized INs (Figure 1A; Booker et al., 2018); cells that were negative for SOM were excluded.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from immunocytochemistry.

claim: Most visualized SOM-INs in rat slices showed characteristic horizontally-oriented dendrites restricted to the str. oriens/alveus.
source: Most visualized SOM-INs in rat slices showed characteristic horizontally-oriented dendrites restricted to the str. oriens/alveus
evidence: This is a direct observation from morphological analysis of recorded cells.

claim: 25 cells (39.7%) possessed an axon projecting to the str. lacunosum-moleculare, consistent with the morphological features of oriens/alveus-lacunosum-moleculare (OLM) INs.
source: and 25 cells (39.7%) possessed an axon projecting to the str. lacunosum-moleculare (Figure 1A), consistent with the morphological features of oriens/alveus-lacunosum-moleculare (OLM) INs as described previously (McBain et al., 1994; Katona et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a direct report of morphological data with citation support.

claim: 2 INs (3.2%) had bistratified axons in str. radiatum and oriens.
source: Further 2 INs (3.2%) had bistratified axons in str. radiatum and oriens
evidence: This is a direct report of morphological data.

claim: 4 INs (6.4%) had axons confined to str. oriens only.
source: 4 (6.4%) had axons confined to str. oriens only.
evidence: This is a direct report of morphological data.

claim: Alveus stimulation produced short-latency EPSCs with an average amplitude of 77.7 ± 16.1 pA in 10 SOM-INs.
source: In the presence of GABAAR antagonists (gabazine or bicuculline, both 10 µM), alveus stimulation produced short-latency EPSCs with an average amplitude of 77.7 ± 16.1 pA (10 cells)
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data.

claim: EPSCs in SOM-INs showed strong facilitation with a paired-pulse ratio (PPR) of 1.8 ± 0.2.
source: and a strong facilitation with a paired-pulse ratio (PPR) of 1.8 ± 0.2 in response to paired-pulses (100 µs, 50 ms interval, Figure 1B), typical of CA1 PC synapses (Lacaille et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with citation support.

claim: Application of baclofen (10 μM) decreased the mean EPSC amplitude by 84% to 12.2 ± 2.2 pA.
source: Application of baclofen (10 μM) decreased the mean EPSC amplitude by 84% to 12.2 ± 2.2 pA (t(d.f.19)=3.96, p=0.001, Holm-Sidak test)
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with statistical analysis.

claim: Baclofen increased the PPR to 2.8 ± 0.5, indicating a reduction in the glutamate release probability at presynaptic terminals by GABABR activation.
source: but increased the PPR to 2.8 ± 0.5 (t(d.f.25)=2.94, p=0.025, Holm-Sidak test, Figure 1C,D) indicating a reduction in the glutamate release probability at presynaptic terminals by GABABR activation.
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with interpretation.

claim: Subsequent CGP (5 μM) application recovered the EPSCs to baseline levels with a mean amplitude of 89.7 ± 13.7 pA.
source: Subsequent CGP (5 μM) application to the bath in a subset of experiments (8 cells) recovered the EPSCs to baseline levels with a mean amplitude of 89.7 ± 13.7 pA (t(d.f.25)=0.68, p=0.502, Holm-Sidak test)
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with statistical analysis.

claim: CGP application recovered the PPR to 1.8 ± 0.2.
source: and PPR of 1.8 ± 0.2 (t(d.f.19)=2.8, p=0.025, Holm-Sidak test, Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with statistical analysis.

claim: NBQX (10 μM) reduced the average EPSC amplitude by 97% to 3.5 ± 1.5 pA, confirming that responses were mediated by glutamatergic synapses.
source: The AMPA receptor (AMPAR) antagonist NBQX (10 μM), applied at the end of a subset of these experiments (5 cells) reduced the average EPSC amplitude by 97% to 3.5 ± 1.5 pA (U(d.f. 4)=0.0, p=0.0006, Mann-Whitney test), confirming that responses were mediated by glutamatergic synapses.
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with interpretation.

claim: In wild-type mice, stimulation of the alveus resulted in an average EPSC amplitude of 62.1 ± 8.5 pA.
source: Under control conditions, stimulation of the alveus resulted in an average EPSC amplitude of 62.1 ± 8.5 pA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data from mouse experiments.

claim: In wild-type mice, bath application of 2 µM baclofen reduced EPSC amplitude by 57% to 26.7 ± 4.9 pA.
source: which following bath application of a low concentration of baclofen (2 µM) was reduced by 57% to 26.7 ± 4.9 pA (F(d.f.2,4)=15.9, p=0.0016, 1-way ANOVA; t = 4.9, p=0.002, Holm-Sidak test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with statistical analysis.

claim: In wild-type mice, subsequent bath application of 5 µM CGP fully reversed the baclofen-induced inhibition to 101.1% of control.
source: Subsequent bath application of 5 µM CGP fully reversed the observed inhibition to 101.1% of control (t = 0.01, p=0.99, Holm-Sidak test).
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with statistical analysis.

claim: Strong presynaptic inhibition is present at inputs onto SOM-INs, irrespective of the species tested.
source: These data confirm that strong presynaptic inhibition is present at inputs onto SOM-INs, irrespective of the species tested.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing rat and mouse data.

claim: Paired-pulse extracellular stimulation to the str. oriens gave rise to large monosynaptic IPSCs with an average amplitude of 158.9 ± 34.4 pA.
source: Paired-pulse extracellular stimulation to the str. oriens proximal to these recorded SOM-INs (9 cells) in the presence of AMPAR and NMDAR antagonists (10 µM NBQX and 50 µM APV) gave rise to large monosynaptic IPSCs with an average amplitude of 158.9 ± 34.4 pA
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data.

claim: IPSCs in SOM-INs showed a depressing PPR of 0.82 ± 0.05.
source: and a depressing PPR of 0.82 ± 0.05 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data.

claim: Activation of GABABRs by bath application of baclofen (10 μM) reduced the IPSC amplitude by 69% to 49.5 ± 13.2 pA.
source: Activation of GABABRs by bath application of baclofen (10 μM) reduced the IPSC amplitude by 69% to 49.5 ± 13.2 pA (t(d.f.16)=5.07, p=0.0003, Holm-Sidak test)
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with statistical analysis.

claim: Baclofen had minimal and non-significant effect on the PPR of IPSCs (0.97 ± 0.05).
source: but had minimal and non-significant effect on the PPR (0.97 ± 0.05; t(d.f.16)=1.58, p=0.251, Holm-Sidak test; Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with statistical analysis.

claim: CGP (5 μM) application recovered the IPSC amplitude to 97% of control levels (154.5 ± 27.7 pA).
source: CGP (5 μM) application recovered the IPSC amplitude to 97% of control levels (154.5 ± 27.7 pA, t(d.f.16)=0.205, p=0.84, Holm-Sidak test; Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with statistical analysis.

claim: Application of bicuculline (10 μM) inhibited the IPSCs by 94% to 9.9 ± 2.1 pA, confirming their GABAAR-mediated nature.
source: Application of bicuculline (10 μM) following CGP recovery inhibited the IPSCs by 94% to 9.9 ± 2.1 pA (U(d.f.9)=0, p=0.0006, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 1D), confirming their GABAAR-mediated nature.
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiological data with interpretation.

claim: Presynaptic GABABRs strongly control the strength of both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs onto CA1 SOM-INs.
source: Thus, our data show that presynaptic GABABRs strongly control the strength of both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs onto CA1 SOM-INs.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the electrophysiological data.

claim: From 42 tested CA1 PC - SOM-IN paired recordings, 5 pairs (12%) showed unitary synaptic coupling.
source: From a total of 42 tested CA1 PC - SOM-IN paired recordings, in 5 pairs (12%) we could observe unitary synaptic coupling in response to a train of presynaptic action potentials (APs) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct report of paired recording data.

claim: No IPSCs elicited by SOM-INs were detected in any of the simultaneously recorded PCs.
source: No IPSCs elicited by SOM-INs were detected in any of the simultaneously recorded PCs.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental observations.

claim: Single APs produced in the presynaptic CA1 PC resulted in short latency unitary EPSCs with an average amplitude of 7.1 ± 1.7 pA (range: 2.5–12.0 pA).
source: Single APs produced in the presynaptic CA1 PC resulted in short latency unitary EPSCs with an average amplitude of 7.1 ± 1.7 pA (range: 2.5–12.0 pA; Figure 2B,C)
evidence: This is a direct report of paired recording data.

claim: Unitary EPSCs had a failure rate of 61.5 ± 7.2% in SOM-INs.
source: and a failure rate of 61.5 ± 7.2% in SOM-INs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct report of paired recording data.

claim: Application of 2 μM baclofen reduced the mean unitary EPSC amplitude by 74% to 1.6 ± 0.9 pA.
source: Application of a lower baclofen concentration (2 μM), reduced the mean EPSC amplitude by 74% to 1.6 ± 0.9 pA (t(d.f. 8)=3.96, p=0.01, Holm-Sidak test; Figure 2B,C)
evidence: This is a direct report of paired recording data with statistical analysis.

claim: Under baclofen, the failure rate increased to 84.8 ± 6.3%, indicating that the release probability was significantly reduced.
source: Under this condition, the failure rate increased to 84.8 ± 6.3% (t(d.f.8)=3.3, p=0.022, Holm-Sidak test; Figure 2D), indicating that the release probability was significantly reduced.
evidence: This is a direct report of paired recording data with interpretation.

claim: Subsequent application of 5 μM CGP recovered both the EPSC amplitude and the failure rate to control levels.
source: Subsequent application of 5 μM CGP recovered both the EPSC amplitude (t(d.f. 8)=0.18, p=0.86, Holm-Sidak test) and the failure rate (t(d.f. 8)=1.35, p=0.21, Holm-Sidak test, Figure 2C,D) to control levels.
evidence: This is a direct report of paired recording data with statistical analysis.

claim: GABABRs strongly inhibit excitatory synaptic inputs from local PCs onto SOM-INs.
source: These data, thus, confirm that GABABRs strongly inhibit excitatory synaptic inputs from local PCs onto SOM-INs
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the paired recording data.

claim: GABABRs have a pivotal role in controlling SOM-IN recruitment in the feedback inhibitory microcircuit.
source: indicating a pivotal role of this receptor in controlling SOM-IN recruitment in this feedback inhibitory microcircuit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: A high surface expression of GABAB1 subunits was consistently observed on presynaptic terminals contacting horizontal, sparsely spiny mGluR1α-immunolabelled dendrites in str. oriens/alveus.
source: We consistently observed a high surface expression of GABAB1 subunits on presynaptic terminals contacting horizontal, sparsely spiny mGluR1α-immunolabelled dendrites in str. oriens/alveus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C)
evidence: This is a direct report of immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: GABAB1 labeling was consistently observed at both VGluT1-positive and VGluT1-negative boutons.
source: We consistently observed GABAB1 labeling at both VGluT1-positive and VGluT1-negative boutons with an apparently higher density of the receptor subunit in VGluT1-negative putative inhibitory terminals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a direct report of immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: 96% of YFP-positive dendritic shafts in the str. oriens (27 out of 28 dendrites) also showed immunoreactivity for mGluR1α.
source: Indeed, by co-labeling for YFP and mGluR1α, we found that 96% of YFP-positive dendritic shafts in the str. oriens (27 out of 28 dendrites) also showed immunoreactivity for this marker glutamate receptor (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a direct report of immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: The surface density of immunogold particles for GABAB1 on YFP-positive dendritic membranes in transgenic mice was 54.61 ± 2.52 particles/µm2.
source: Furthermore, the surface density of immunogold particles for GABAB1 on YFP-positive dendritic membranes in double-labelled replicas from the transgenic mice was comparable to that previously found in mGluR1α-positive SOM-IN dendrites from rat hippocampal CA1 (54.61 ± 2.52 particles/µm2 on YFP-positive mouse dendrites, Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 49.1 ± 4.5 particles/µm2 in mGluR1α-positive rat dendrites; Booker et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: The surface density of GABAB1 in mGluR1α-positive rat SOM-IN dendrites was 49.1 ± 4.5 particles/µm2.
source: Furthermore, the surface density of immunogold particles for GABAB1 on YFP-positive dendritic membranes in double-labelled replicas from the transgenic mice was comparable to that previously found in mGluR1α-positive SOM-IN dendrites from rat hippocampal CA1 (54.61 ± 2.52 particles/µm2 on YFP-positive mouse dendrites, Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 49.1 ± 4.5 particles/µm2 in mGluR1α-positive rat dendrites; Booker et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a citation to previous data.

claim: An abundant surface expression of GABAB1 was observed on presynaptic terminals in contact with YFP-positive dendritic shafts of SOM-INs in the str. oriens in mice.
source: In good agreement with the findings from rat, we observed an abundant surface expression of the receptor subunit on presynaptic terminals in contact with YFP-positive dendritic shafts of SOM-INs in the str. oriens in the mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct report of immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: Immunoparticles for GABAB1 were mainly confined to, and distributed non-homogeneously over, the active zones (AZs) of terminals.
source: Immunoparticles for GABAB1 were mainly confined to, and distributed non-homogeneously over, the active zones (AZs) of terminals (Figure 3B,C)
evidence: This is a direct report of immunoelectron microscopy observations.

claim: GABAB1 receptor subunits were occasionally seen along the extrasynaptic membrane of presynaptic boutons.
source: Furthermore, receptor subunits were occasionally seen along the extrasynaptic membrane of presynaptic boutons (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is a direct report of immunoelectron microscopy observations.

claim: Immunoreactivity for GABAB1 was significantly higher in VGAT-positive and VGluT1-negative inhibitory terminals (43.00 ± 6.61 particles/µm2, n = 36) compared to VGAT-negative and VGluT1-positive excitatory presumed PC axon terminals (17.36 ± 2.13 particles/µm2, n = 60; p<0.0001).
source: In these replicas, we consistently observed labeling for GABAB1 in both populations of terminals, but immunoreactivity for the receptor subunit was significantly higher in VGAT-positive and VGluT1-negative inhibitory terminals (43.00 ± 6,61 particles/µm2, n = 36) compared to VGAT-negative and VGluT1-positive excitatory presumed PC axon terminals (17.36 ± 2.13 particles/µm2, n = 60; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney test; Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative immunoelectron microscopy data with statistical analysis.

claim: Both GABAergic and glutamatergic terminals forming synapses onto SOM-INs contain large numbers of GABABRs.
source: These data demonstrate that both GABAergic and glutamatergic terminals forming synapses onto SOM-INs contain large numbers of GABABRs, consistent with electrophysiological findings demonstrating a robust presynaptic inhibition at inhibitory and excitatory inputs
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: There is a substantial difference in the surface density of GABABRs between GABAergic and glutamatergic bouton populations contacting SOM-INs.
source: however, with a substantial difference in the surface density between the two bouton populations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the quantitative immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SOM-IN axons in the str. lacunosum-moleculare resulted in temporally-aligned IPSCs in CA1 PCs with an average peak amplitude of 14.0 ± 3.6 pA (6 cells).
source: Optogenetic activation of SOM-IN axons in the str. lacunosum-moleculare resulted in temporally-aligned IPSCs in CA1 PCs with an average peak amplitude of 14.0 ± 3.6 pA (6 cells, Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a direct report of optogenetic electrophysiology data.

claim: Baclofen application markedly reduced the optically-evoked IPSC amplitudes by 61% to 5.3 ± 1.3 pA, indicating the presence of presynaptic GABABRs at SOM-IN output synapses.
source: Baclofen application markedly reduced the optically-evoked IPSC amplitudes by 61% to 5.3 ± 1.3 pA (t(d.f. 8)=4.31, p=0.007, Holm-Sidak test, Figure 5B,C) indicating the presence of presynaptic GABABRs at SOM-IN output synapses.
evidence: This is a direct report of optogenetic electrophysiology data with interpretation.

claim: Subsequent CGP bath-application (4 cells) recovered the IPSC amplitude to 119% of control (15.2 ± 3.4 pA).
source: Subsequent CGP bath-application (4 cells) recovered the IPSC amplitude to 119% of control (15.2 ± 3.4 pA, t(d.f. 8)=0.12, p=0.90, Holm-Sidak test, Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a direct report of optogenetic electrophysiology data with statistical analysis.

claim: GABABR activation produced a strong whole-cell current of 49 ± 15 pA postsynaptically (6 cells), plausibly due to Kir3 channel opening in CA1 PC dendrites.
source: However, GABABR activation also produced a strong IWC of 49 ± 15 pA postsynaptically (6 cells, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), plausibly due to Kir3 channel opening in CA1 PC dendrites (Degro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiology data with inference based on citation.

claim: Pre-application of SCH-23,390 (10 µM) reduced the baclofen-induced whole-cell current in CA1 PCs to 19 ± 3 pA (7 cells).
source: Pre-application of SCH reduced the baclofen-induced IWC in CA1 PCs to 19 ± 3 pA (7 cells, t(d.f. 11)=1, p=0.002, Mann-Whitney test, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct report of electrophysiology data with statistical analysis.

claim: In the presence of SCH, the IPSC elicited by optogenetic activation of SOM-IN axons had an average amplitude of 7.0 ± 1.3 pA.
source: In the presence of SCH, the IPSC elicited by optogenetic activation of SOM-IN axons had an average amplitude of 7.0 ± 1.3 pA (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is a direct report of optogenetic electrophysiology data.

claim: Baclofen application in the presence of SCH inhibited the IPSC by 70% to 2.3 ± 0.4 pA.
source: Baclofen application under this condition inhibited the IPSC by 70% to 2.3 ± 0.4 pA (t(d.f. 7)=4.82, p=0.002, Holm-Sidak test, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a direct report of optogenetic electrophysiology data with statistical analysis.

claim: The baclofen-induced presynaptic inhibition of SOM-INs IPSCs in the presence of SCH was comparable to that of baclofen applied alone.
source: The baclofen-induced presynaptic inhibition of SOM-INs IPSCs in the presence of SCH was comparable to that of baclofen applied alone (t(d.f. 14)=0.2, p=0.84, Holm-Sidak test, Figure 5E)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical comparison of electrophysiology data.

claim: The observed reduction in the IPSC amplitude was not contaminated by a Kir3-mediated postsynaptic shunting effect in the PCs.
source: indicating that the observed reduction in the IPSC amplitude was not contaminated by a Kir3-mediated postsynaptic shunting effect in the PCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of baclofen effects with and without SCH.

claim: GABABRs are present in the axon terminals of SOM-INs and strongly inhibit the synaptic output of these INs.
source: These data, thus, confirm that GABABRs are present in the axon terminals of SOM-INs and strongly inhibit the synaptic output of these INs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the optogenetic electrophysiology data.

claim: There was no significant difference in the density of immunoparticles for GABAB1 on YFP-positive terminals (45.57 ± 2.31 particles/µm2, n = 66) of SOM-INs and YFP-negative putative PC boutons (41.56 ± 4.71/µm2, n = 41; p=0.099).
